title: Stone Dragon
subtitle: Stone and earth stretched across a restless frontier

chapters.label: CHAPTER 01 · EARLY BARRIERS
chapters.heading: Stone and earth rose against the steppe winds.
chapters.subheading: First state walls of the Warring States.
chapters.body: During the Spring and Autumn and Warring States periods the states of Zheng, Chu, Qin and others built extensive stone or rammed-earth fortifications to repel swords and spears. The Qin ruler unified the realm in 221 BC, ordered the demolition of rival walls and then began linking the remaining sections to face the Xiongnu from the north.

chapters.label: CHAPTER 02 · MING REFORGE
chapters.heading: Bricks and towers marked a new resolve.
chapters.subheading: Ming walls reinforced the northern edge.
chapters.body: After defeat at the Battle of Tumu the Ming dynasty built stronger walls using bricks and stone, especially near Beijing. Up to 25,000 watchtowers were erected. Between 1567 and 1570 General Qi Jiguang oversaw the construction of 1,200 watchtowers from Shanhaiguan Pass to Changping, reinforcing the frontier against Mongol raids.

chapters.label: CHAPTER 03 · FINAL BREACH
chapters.heading: The wall finally yielded to a new empire.
chapters.subheading: Manchu crossing ends the Ming stand.
chapters.body: The Manchu forces crossed the Great Wall in 1644 after Beijing had fallen to Li Zicheng. Earlier they had raided across the barrier many times, but this crossing marked a decisive conquest. The gates at Shanhai Pass were opened on May 25 by General Wu Sangui, aligning with the Manchus to retake the capital.
